newsitem.title: PERU: Peruvian, Japanese leaders to discuss hostages.
newsitem.headline: Peruvian, Japanese leaders to discuss hostages.

text.p: Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto agreed on Wednesday to an urgent meeting this weekend in Canada to discuss the six-week-old Peruvian hostage crisis.

The meeting in Toronto on Saturday is a sign of growing concern in Lima and Tokyo that the siege at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima could continue and endanger the lives of 72 captives held by Marxist rebels.
"President Fujimori has told us he wants to discuss the Peruvian situation with me as soon as possible," Hashimoto told reporters in Japan.

Japanese leaders this week expressed concern that Fujimori is taking chances with the hostages' lives by stepping up psychological pressure on the roughly 15 armed members of the Marxist Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA).
In an apparent bid to weaken the rebels' resolve, police have blasted early morning marching music at the residence and led processions of armoured vehicles around it.

The MRTA rebels, who have mined and booby-trapped the diplomatic compound, fired several bullets on Monday at police aboard a convoy of armoured cars and hit one vehicle, narrowly missing policemen inside.

"He will not meet with Hashimoto to apologise for the police attitude nor is he going to Canada to ask permission (from Japan) to enter the residence (by force)," a senior government official told Reuters.
The official, who requested anonymity, added that Fujimori would travel to Washington after the Toronto meeting "to thank President (Bill) Clinton for his support."

The Canadian government said on Wednesday the nation was chosen as the venue because the Canadian Ambassador to Peru Anthony Vincent was on a "guarantor" peace panel which it was hoped would mediate talks between the rebels and Peru's government.

"Canada has been chosen for the site of this meeting because of its role as a member of the Commission of Guarantor and the convenience of its location for both leaders," a statement from Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien said.
Efforts to start talks with the MRTA guerrillas have stalled over the main rebel demand of freedom for about 400 jailed comrades, which Fujimori has refused to discuss.
The other members of the guarantor commission are Michel Minnig, the Lima head of the International Committee of the Red Cross, and Roman Catholic bishop Juan Luis Cipriani.
Both sides have accepted in principle the panel's role in the crisis, but the MRTA insists on also including a European government representative.
Isaac Velazco, the MRTA's international spokesman, told Reuters by telephone from Hamburg, that Hashimoto in his meeting with Fujimori should demand a "political solution" to the siege.

"If Japan really wants to guarantee the safety of its nationals held at the residence, it should use its influence and economic power so that Fujimori respects what is Japanese territory and it should demand a political solution to the occupation," Velazco said.
Aid workers and police say that most hostages are being treated for such conditions as hypertension, digestive ailments or depression.

The MRTA rebels, who take the name for their movement from an 18th century Indian leader who led an uprising against Spanish colonial rule, orginally seized hundreds of guests when they stormed a garden party at the residence Dec. 17.

They released most of the captives but kept those they consider the most important bargaining chips, including two Peruvian ministers, generals, security chiefs, about two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats and the Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors.
